power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "P=0.113", Sentence = "A linear WHtR interaction was also observed for ischemic stroke (P=0.010; Benjamini-Hochberg-adjusted P=0.027), although the flexible-age spline interaction test did not support heterogeneity (P=0.113)."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

text.text: Waist-to-height ratio (WHtR) scales waist circumference to stature.

Meta-analyses and prospective studies suggest that WHtR identifies cardiometabolic risk at least as well as BMI and other anthropometric measures (Ashwell et al., 2009; Ashwell et al., 2012; Savva et al., 2013; Gelber et al., 2008; Jayedi et al., 2022; Feng et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Meta-analyses and prospective studies suggest that WHtR identifies cardiometabolic risk at least as well as BMI and other anthropometric measures <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Ashwell et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Ashwell et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Savva et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Gelber et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Jayedi et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Feng et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The UK National Institute for Health and Care Excellence, recommends WHtR alongside BMI <35 kg/m 2 , identifying 0.50 as a practical boundary for increased central adiposity (NICE, 2026).
text.formatted: The UK National Institute for Health and Care Excellence, recommends WHtR alongside BMI <35 kg/m 2 , identifying 0.50 as a practical boundary for increased central adiposity <ref type="bibr">(NICE, 2026</ref>).

text.text: An important question remains unresolved: does WHtR identify prospective disease risk that is meaningfully missed when BMI is used to classify apparently normal weight adults?
Most WHtR studies address prevalent risk factors, individual outcomes, or mortality.

Although waist circumference and waist-to-hip ratio identify cardiovascular risk heterogeneity within BMI categories, comparable longitudinal evidence for WHtR across multiple outcomes remains limited (Dardari et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Although waist circumference and waist-to-hip ratio identify cardiovascular risk heterogeneity within BMI categories, comparable longitudinal evidence for WHtR across multiple outcomes remains limited <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Dardari et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Using data from the All of Us Research Program (AoURP), we evaluated WHtR associations with eight incident cardiometabolic outcomes, emphasizing risk among normal-BMI adults, nonlinear relationships, standardized event probabilities, and incremental discrimination beyond BMI (AoURP Investigators, 2019).
We conducted a longitudinal study using AoURP Registered Tier Curated Data
The index date was the first numeric AoURP-computed waist measurement.

Eligible adults were aged ≥18 years, had valid same-day waist and height measurements, met anthropometric quality-control criteria, and had ≥365 days of pre-index observation to ascertain prevalent disease.
The longitudinal cohort included 308,600 participants.
Sex-adjusted analyses included participants recorded as female or male; other categories had insufficient numbers for stable outcome-specific estimation.
Each outcome-specific risk set excluded the corresponding prevalent disease on or before baseline.
BMI-WHtR phenotypes could be assigned to 308,218 participants; 382 lacked valid analytic BMI (Supplemental Figure S1; Supplemental Table S1).
text.formatted: BMI-WHtR phenotypes could be assigned to 308,218 participants; 382 lacked valid analytic BMI (Supplemental Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">S1</ref>; Supplemental Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">S1</ref>).

text.text: Program-computed waist circumference is the mean of the two closest measurements.
WHtR was waist circumference divided by same-day height, both in centimeters.
BMI used the program-computed measure; BMI calculated from same-day height and weight showed near-perfect agreement.
Prespecified cohort-entry anthropometric quality-control limits were 120 to 220 cm height and 40 to 200 cm waist circumference.
BMI values from 10 to 80 kg/m 2 were considered valid for BMI-based analyses; BMI validity was assessed separately from eligibility for the longitudinal anthropometric cohort.
BMI was categorized as underweight (<18.5 kg/m 2 ), normal weight (18.5 to <25 kg/m 2 ), overweight (25 to <30 kg/m 2 ), or obesity (≥30 kg/m 2 ).
text.formatted: BMI was categorized as underweight (<18.5 kg/m 2 ), normal weight (18.5 to <25 kg/m 2 ), overweight (25 to <30 kg/m 2 ), or obesity (≥30 kg/m 2 ).

text.text: For BMI-WHtR discordance analyses, elevated WHtR was defined a priori as ≥0.50.
Thresholds of 0.52 and 0.55 were evaluated in sensitivity analyses and were not selected through outcome-specific optimization.

We evaluated eight incident outcomes: type 2 diabetes (T2D), hypertension, ischemic heart disease (IHD), myocardial infarction (MI), ischemic stroke, heart failure (HF), atrial fibrillation (AF), and chronic kidney disease (CKD).
Outcomes were constructed from standardized OMOP condition concepts and clinically relevant descendants.
Concept hierarchies were adjudicated before outcome construction to distinguish concepts suitable for identifying prevalent disease from those suitable for initiating an incident event.

Pregnancy-related conditions, historical or status concepts, procedural diagnoses, and other concepts not representing new-onset clinical disease were excluded from incident definitions, as appropriate.
For each outcome, participants with corresponding prevalent disease on or before the index date were excluded.
An incident event was defined as the first qualifying diagnosis after the index date (Supplemental Table S2).
text.formatted: An incident event was defined as the first qualifying diagnosis after the index date (Supplemental Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">S2</ref>).

text.text: Follow-up extended from baseline to the first qualifying outcome, observation end, or death, whichever occurred first.
Events recorded on the date of death were retained because within-day temporal ordering could not be established and terminal diagnoses may represent legitimate clinical events.
Diagnoses recorded after death were excluded.
Primary models therefore estimated cause-specific hazards for each incident cardiometabolic outcome.
Within each fully adjusted analytic population, follow-up was summarized as median (IQR), and persontime was summed from baseline to the first event or censoring.

Models adjusted for baseline age, sex, continuous BMI, race, ethnicity, smoking (never, former, current), education (<high school, high school, vocational training, college graduate/advanced degree), and household income using available AoURP categories.
text.formatted: Models adjusted for baseline age, sex, continuous BMI, race, ethnicity, smoking (never, former, current), education (<high school, high school, vocational training, college graduate/advanced degree), and household income using available AoURP categories.

text.text: Analyses used R in the Researcher Workbench.
Baseline characteristics were summarized overall and by BMI-WHtR phenotype as mean (SD) or n (%), without between-group hypothesis tests.
Whole-cohort analyses evaluated continuous/nonlinear WHtR associations and incremental discrimination in outcome-specific complete-case risk sets.
Normal-BMI analyses evaluated WHtR ≥0.50 versus <0.50 and standardized event probabilities.
text.formatted: Normal-BMI analyses evaluated WHtR ≥0.50 versus <0.50 and standardized event probabilities.

text.text: WHtR was initially modeled continuously, with hazard ratios (HRs) reported per 0.05-unit higher WHtR; estimates per 1-SD higher WHtR were also calculated.
Nonlinear associations were evaluated using restricted cubic splines with 4 knots placed at approximately the 5th, 35th, 65th, and 95th percentiles of the WHtR distribution.
WHtR 0.50 was used as the graphical reference value.
Likelihood-ratio tests compared nonlinear with linear model specifications.
To evaluate discordance between BMI and central adiposity, analyses were restricted to adults with normal BMI (18.5 to <25 kg/m 2 ).
text.formatted: To evaluate discordance between BMI and central adiposity, analyses were restricted to adults with normal BMI (18.5 to <25 kg/m 2 ).

text.text: WHtR ≥0.50 was compared with WHtR <0.50.
text.formatted: WHtR ≥0.50 was compared with WHtR <0.50.

text.text: Continuous BMI was retained to reduce residual confounding by body size within the normal-BMI range.
Additional exploratory analyses evaluated whether continuous WHtR associations differed across normal-BMI, overweight, and obesity categories.
Participants with underweight BMI were excluded.
Cause-specific Cox models included BMI-category-specific baseline hazards, WHtR expressed per 0.05-unit increment, and WHtR-by-BMI-category interaction terms.
Models retained continuous BMI and the other adjustment covariates, whose coefficients were shared across BMI categories.
BMI-specific WHtR estimates and pairwise ratios of hazard ratios were derived from the same interaction model.
Two-degree-of-freedom likelihood-ratio tests compared models with and without the interaction terms.
Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment was applied across the eight outcome-specific omnibus interaction tests separately within each age specification.
Pairwise comparisons used two-sided Wald tests and were interpreted as exploratory without multiplicity adjustment (Supplemental Tables S3 and S4).
text.formatted: Pairwise comparisons used two-sided Wald tests and were interpreted as exploratory without multiplicity adjustment (Supplemental Tables <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">S3</ref> and <ref type="table">S4</ref>).

text.text: For exploratory nonlinear interaction analyses, WHtR was represented using a natural cubic spline with internal knots at the outcome-specific pooled 35th and 65th percentiles and boundary knots at the 5th and 95th percentiles.
Six-degree-of-freedom likelihood-ratio tests compared models with a common WHtR spline association against models allowing BMIcategory-specific associations.
Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment was applied separately across the eight outcome-specific spline interaction tests within each age specification.
Sensitivity analyses represented age using a natural cubic spline with 4 degrees of freedom (Supplemental Tables S3 and S5).
text.formatted: Sensitivity analyses represented age using a natural cubic spline with 4 degrees of freedom (Supplemental Tables <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">S3</ref> and <ref type="table">S5</ref>).

text.text: Nested Cox models compared the covariate model, including BMI, against models adding linear or spline WHtR.
Fixed participant-level 5-fold cross-validation retained identical fold assignments across outcomes.
Spline parameters were estimated within training sets to prevent leakage.
Harrell's C-index was calculated in held-out participants, with changes interpreted by magnitude and consistency (Supplemental Table S6).
text.formatted: Harrell's C-index was calculated in held-out participants, with changes interpreted by magnitude and consistency (Supplemental Table <ref type="table">S6</ref>).

text.text: Among normal-BMI adults, standardized 3-year event probabilities were estimated by predicting each participant's probability under WHtR <0.50 and ≥0.50, retaining observed covariates, then averaging predictions.
text.formatted: Among normal-BMI adults, standardized 3-year event probabilities were estimated by predicting each participant's probability under WHtR <0.50 and ≥0.50, retaining observed covariates, then averaging predictions.

text.text: These cause-specific Cox estimates are model-based probabilities, not competing-risk cumulative-incidence estimates or causal contrasts.
Primary fully adjusted analyses used complete covariate data.
Missing baseline covariates were addressed using multiple imputation with 20 imputations as a sensitivity analysis.
Additional analyses evaluated WHtR thresholds of 0.50, 0.52, and 0.55.

A 365-day landmark analysis excluded participants who experienced the outcome or were censored during the first year after baseline to reduce potential influence from occult prevalent disease or near-term diagnostic ascertainment.
Follow-up for retained participants was measured from day 365.
Landmark analyses evaluated continuous WHtR in the whole cohort and WHtR ≥0.50 versus <0.50 among adults with normal BMI.
text.formatted: Landmark analyses evaluated continuous WHtR in the whole cohort and WHtR ≥0.50 versus <0.50 among adults with normal BMI.

text.text: Proportional-hazards assumptions were assessed using Schoenfeld residuals.
As WHtR-specific nonproportionality was observed for hypertension and AF, interval-specific models estimated associations during 0 to 2 years and >2 years of follow-up.
text.formatted: As WHtR-specific nonproportionality was observed for hypertension and AF, interval-specific models estimated associations during 0 to 2 years and >2 years of follow-up.

text.text: All hypothesis tests were 2-sided.
Given the related outcomes and emphasis on estimation, findings were interpreted according to magnitude, precision, consistency, and robustness rather than binary statistical significance alone.

Age sensitivity analyses replaced linear age with a natural cubic spline (4 degrees of freedom), retaining the same complete-case populations for continuous WHtR and the normal-BMI WHtR ≥0.50 contrast.
Likelihood-ratio tests assessed sex-by-WHtR interactions, with sex-specific estimates from separate adjusted models, for continuous WHtR and the normal-BMI threshold contrast.
Exploratory omnibus tests assessed race/ethnicity interactions in categories with adequate participants and events.
Interpretation considered multiplicity, statistical power, and the social and contextual meaning of these classifications.
The final longitudinal anthropometric cohort included 308,600 adults; 305,341 participants recorded as female or male were eligible for sex-adjusted inferential analyses.
Before outcome-specific exclusions for prevalent disease, 207,346 participants had complete data for all fully adjusted covariates.
Among 308,218 participants with sufficient anthropometric data for BMI-WHtR phenotype classification, 77,684 had normal BMI: 53,383 had WHtR <0.50 and 24,301 had WHtR ≥0.50.
text.formatted: Among 308,218 participants with sufficient anthropometric data for BMI-WHtR phenotype classification, 77,684 had normal BMI: 53,383 had WHtR <0.50 and 24,301 had WHtR ≥0.50.

text.text: Thus, 31.3% of adults with normal BMI had WHtR ≥0.50.

Among participants with normal BMI, those with WHtR ≥0.50 were older than those with WHtR <0.50 (mean age, 59.1 versus 47.0 years) and had greater waist circumference (89.2 versus 76.1 cm), despite a smaller difference in BMI (23.4 versus 22.0 kg/m²) (Table 1; Supplemental Table S1).

Total follow-up ranged from 354,405 person-years for hypertension to 649,934 person-years for ischemic stroke.

A small number of diagnoses recorded after death were excluded from the outcome-specific analysis.

Higher WHtR was associated with increased risk of each cardiometabolic outcome after adjustment for age, sex, BMI, race, ethnicity, smoking status, educational attainment, and household income.
Per 0.05-unit higher WHtR, the largest association was observed for T2D (hazard ratio [HR], 1.31; 95% CI, 1.29-1.34).

Positive associations were also observed for MI (HR, 1.20; 95% CI, 1.15-1.25), ischemic stroke (HR, 1.16; 95% CI, 1.12-1.20), heart failure (HF; HR, 1.16; 95% CI, 1.14-1.19), chronic kidney disease (CKD; HR, 1.16; 95% CI, 1.13-1.18), IHD (HR, 1.14; 95% CI, 1.11-1.17), and hypertension (HR, 1.14; 95% CI, 1.13-1.16).
The association with atrial fibrillation (AF) was smaller but remained positive (HR, 1.07; 95% CI, 1.04-1.09) (Table 2; Figure 1).

text.text: Corresponding HRs per 1-SD higher WHtR were 1.77 for T2D, 1.33 for hypertension, 1.31 for IHD, 1.47 for MI, 1.36 for ischemic stroke, 1.37 for HF, 1.14 for AF, and 1.36 for CKD (Table 2).

text.text: Restricted cubic spline analyses demonstrated heterogeneous exposure-response relationships across outcomes.
Evidence of nonlinearity was strongest for T2D, hypertension, HF, and AF; additional evidence was observed for IHD and CKD, whereas evidence was weaker for MI and ischemic stroke.
Tests for nonlinearity ranged from P<0.001 for several outcomes to P=0.041 for ischemic stroke.
text.formatted: Tests for nonlinearity ranged from P<0.001 for several outcomes to P=0.041 for ischemic stroke.

text.text: T2D and hypertension risks increased nonlinearly at higher WHtR values.
IHD, MI, ischemic stroke, and CKD generally showed increasing hazards with higher WHtR.
In contrast, HF and AF showed more curvilinear associations, with the lowest estimated hazards near the middle of the WHtR distribution.
These findings indicate that WHtR associations cannot be fully characterized by a single linear coefficient or universal dichotomous threshold (Figure 2; Supplemental Table S9).
text.formatted: These findings indicate that WHtR associations cannot be fully characterized by a single linear coefficient or universal dichotomous threshold (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">2</ref>; Supplemental Table <ref type="table">S9</ref>).

text.text: Among normal-BMI adults, WHtR ≥0.50 versus <0.50 was associated with all eight outcomes after adjustment including continuous BMI (Table 3).
text.formatted: Among normal-BMI adults, WHtR ≥0.50 versus <0.50 was associated with all eight outcomes after adjustment including continuous BMI (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">3</ref>).

text.text: The largest associations were observed for T2D (HR, 1.74; 95% CI, 1.49-2.03), ischemic stroke (HR, 1.52; 95% CI, 1.27-1.83), and MI (HR, 1.49; 95% CI, 1.19-1.87).

Elevated WHtR was also associated with IHD (HR, 1.31; 95% CI, 1.14-1.51), CKD (HR, 1.31; 95% CI, 1.16-1.49), hypertension (HR, 1.26; 95% CI, 1.16-1.37), AF (HR, 1.26; 95% CI, 1.09-1.45), and HF (HR, 1.24; 95% CI, 1.07-1.43) (Table 3).

text.text: Standardized 3-year event probabilities were higher with WHtR ≥0.50 across all outcomes.
For WHtR <0.50 versus ≥0.50, probabilities were 1.24% versus 2.14% for T2D, 0.58% versus 0.86% for MI, and 0.80% versus 1.21% for ischemic stroke (Figure 3).
text.formatted: For WHtR <0.50 versus ≥0.50, probabilities were 1.24% versus 2.14% for T2D, 0.58% versus 0.86% for MI, and 0.80% versus 1.21% for ischemic stroke (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">3</ref>).

text.text: In additional interaction analyses, the association between continuous WHtR and incident diabetes differed across BMI categories.

Adjusted HRs per 0.05-unit higher WHtR were 1.52 (95% CI, 1.43-1.61) among adults with normal BMI, 1.42 (1.36-1.49) among those with overweight, and 1.22 (1.20-1.25) among those with obesity (P for interaction <0.001) (Supplemental Table S3).
text.formatted: Adjusted HRs per 0.05-unit higher WHtR were 1.52 (95% CI, 1.43-1.61) among adults with normal BMI, 1.42 (1.36-1.49) among those with overweight, and 1.22 (1.20-1.25) among those with obesity (P for interaction <0.001) (Supplemental Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">S3</ref>).

text.text: The diabetes association was stronger in normal BMI than obesity (ratio of HRs, 1.24; 95% CI, 1.17-1.32), whereas the comparison with overweight was inconclusive (1.07; 0.99-1.15) (Supplemental Table S4).
text.formatted: The diabetes association was stronger in normal BMI than obesity (ratio of HRs, 1.24; 95% CI, 1.17-1.32), whereas the comparison with overweight was inconclusive (1.07; 0.99-1.15) (Supplemental Table <ref type="table">S4</ref>).

text.text: Hypertension associations also differed across BMI categories.
Corresponding HRs were 1.27 (95% CI, 1.22-1.31), 1.18 (1.14-1.21), and 1.08 (1.06-1.10), respectively (P for interaction <0.001).
text.formatted: Corresponding HRs were 1.27 (95% CI, 1.22-1.31), 1.18 (1.14-1.21), and 1.08 (1.06-1.10), respectively (P for interaction <0.001).

text.text: The normal-BMI association was stronger than those in both overweight and obesity (Supplemental Table S4).
text.formatted: The normal-BMI association was stronger than those in both overweight and obesity (Supplemental Table <ref type="table">S4</ref>).

text.text: Diabetes and hypertension omnibus interaction tests remained significant after Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment, and findings were similar with flexible age adjustment (Supplemental Table S3).
text.formatted: Diabetes and hypertension omnibus interaction tests remained significant after Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment, and findings were similar with flexible age adjustment (Supplemental Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">S3</ref>).

text.text: A linear WHtR interaction was also observed for ischemic stroke (P=0.010; Benjamini-Hochberg-adjusted P=0.027), although the flexible-age spline interaction test did not support heterogeneity (P=0.113).
Exploratory spline interaction analyses supported heterogeneity for diabetes and hypertension under both age specifications.
Additional evidence was observed for myocardial infarction, heart failure, and chronic kidney disease, but these tests do not establish uniformly stronger associations in normal-BMI adults.
The linear-age stroke spline interaction model produced a convergence warning and was not interpreted (Supplemental Tables S3 and S5).
text.formatted: The linear-age stroke spline interaction model produced a convergence warning and was not interpreted (Supplemental Tables <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">S3</ref> and <ref type="table">S5</ref>).

text.text: Adding nonlinear WHtR improved mean cross-validated discrimination for all eight outcomes.
The largest gain was for T2D, with C-index increasing from 0.7343 to 0.7477 (ΔC=0.0134).
Gains for other outcomes ranged from 0.0009 for AF to 0.0052 for MI.
Linear WHtR provided similar gains for most outcomes, with greater benefits from nonlinear modeling for HF and IHD (Supplemental Table S6).
text.formatted: Linear WHtR provided similar gains for most outcomes, with greater benefits from nonlinear modeling for HF and IHD (Supplemental Table <ref type="table">S6</ref>).

text.text: Associations were similar after exclusion of the first 365 days of follow-up.

Per 0.05-unit higher WHtR, landmark HRs were 1.31 for T2D, 1.12 for hypertension, 1.13 for IHD, 1.19 for MI, 1.20 for ischemic stroke, 1.15 for HF, 1.06 for AF, and 1.14 for CKD (Supplemental Table S9).
text.formatted: Per 0.05-unit higher WHtR, landmark HRs were 1.31 for T2D, 1.12 for hypertension, 1.13 for IHD, 1.19 for MI, 1.20 for ischemic stroke, 1.15 for HF, 1.06 for AF, and 1.14 for CKD (Supplemental Table <ref type="table">S9</ref>).

text.text: Among adults with normal BMI, associations between WHtR ≥0.50 and all eight outcomes persisted in the 365-day landmark analyses.

Adjusted HRs were 1.68 (95% CI, 1.39-2.03) for diabetes, 1.20 (1.08-1.32) for hypertension, 1.28 (1.09-1.50) for ischemic heart disease, 1.40 (1.08-1.82) for myocardial infarction, 1.62 (1.31-2.00) for ischemic stroke, 1.21 (1.03-1.43) for heart failure, 1.28 (1.09-1.50) for atrial fibrillation, and 1.19 (1.03-1.38) for chronic kidney disease (Supplemental Table S10).

text.text: Alternative dichotomous thresholds produced outcome-dependent findings.

For T2D, hypertension, IHD, MI, ischemic stroke, and CKD, elevated WHtR generally identified higher risk across thresholds of 0.50, 0.52, and 0.55; HF associations strengthened at higher thresholds, whereas AF showed little or no excess risk at lower thresholds despite a positive continuous association (Supplemental Figure S2; Supplemental Table S11).
text.formatted: For T2D, hypertension, IHD, MI, ischemic stroke, and CKD, elevated WHtR generally identified higher risk across thresholds of 0.50, 0.52, and 0.55; HF associations strengthened at higher thresholds, whereas AF showed little or no excess risk at lower thresholds despite a positive continuous association (Supplemental Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">S2</ref>; Supplemental Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">S11</ref>).

text.text: WHtR-specific proportional-hazards assumptions were generally supported; evidence of nonproportionality was observed for hypertension and AF (Supplemental Table S12).
text.formatted: WHtR-specific proportional-hazards assumptions were generally supported; evidence of nonproportionality was observed for hypertension and AF (Supplemental Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">S12</ref>).

text.text: For hypertension, the adjusted HR per 0.05-unit higher WHtR was 1.17 (95% CI, 1.14-1.19) during the first 2 years and 1.11 (95% CI, 1.09-1.14) thereafter.
Corresponding HRs for AF were 1.08 (95% CI, 1.04-1.12) and 1.05 (95% CI, 1.02-1.09), respectively.
Associations therefore attenuated but remained positive during later follow-up (Supplemental Table S13).
text.formatted: Associations therefore attenuated but remained positive during later follow-up (Supplemental Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">S13</ref>).

text.text: Multiple-imputation results were highly consistent with complete-case analyses.
HRs per 1-SD higher WHtR were 1.75 for T2D, 1.32 for hypertension, 1.29 for IHD, 1.47 for MI, 1.37 for ischemic stroke, 1.41 for HF, 1.15 for AF, and 1.36 for CKD (Supplemental Table S14).
text.formatted: HRs per 1-SD higher WHtR were 1.75 for T2D, 1.32 for hypertension, 1.29 for IHD, 1.47 for MI, 1.37 for ischemic stroke, 1.41 for HF, 1.15 for AF, and 1.36 for CKD (Supplemental Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">S14</ref>).

text.text: Associations were robust to flexible adjustment for age.

When age was modeled using a natural cubic spline with 4 degrees of freedom, adjusted HRs per 0.05-unit higher WHtR ranged from 1.07 (95% CI, 1.04-1.09) for atrial fibrillation to 1.31 (95% CI, 1.29-1.34) for type 2 diabetes, closely reproducing the primary estimates.

Among adults with normal BMI, flexible age adjustment similarly preserved the associations between WHtR ≥0.50 and all eight outcomes, including type 2 diabetes (HR, 1.75; 95% CI, 1.50-2.05), myocardial infarction (HR, 1.50; 95% CI, 1.20-1.88), and ischemic stroke (HR, 1.52; 95% CI, 1.26-1.83).
These findings indicate that the principal associations were not materially altered by allowing a nonlinear relationship between age and disease risk (Supplemental Table S15).
text.formatted: These findings indicate that the principal associations were not materially altered by allowing a nonlinear relationship between age and disease risk (Supplemental Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">S15</ref>).

text.text: Sex-stratified analyses demonstrated associations between higher continuous WHtR and all eight outcomes in both females and males.

Evidence of a sex interaction was observed for type 2 diabetes (P for interaction=0.003), although the sex-specific estimates were similar in magnitude (HR per 0.05-unit higher WHtR, 1.31 [95% CI, 1.28-1.34] in females and 1.29 [95% CI, 1.25-1.34] in males).
No other continuous WHtR association showed a statistically significant sex interaction.
Among adults with normal BMI, there was no statistically significant sex interaction for the WHtR ≥0.50 contrast for any outcome.

Exploratory omnibus tests identified race-by-WHtR interactions for type 2 diabetes, hypertension, heart failure, and chronic kidney disease, whereas no statistically significant ethnicity-by-WHtR interactions were detected.
These exploratory findings require further evaluation and should not be interpreted as evidence of intrinsic biological differences between demographic groups (Supplemental Tables S15 and S16).
text.formatted: These exploratory findings require further evaluation and should not be interpreted as evidence of intrinsic biological differences between demographic groups (Supplemental Tables <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">S15</ref> and <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">S16</ref>).

text.text: WHtR identified cardiometabolic risk beyond BMI classification, including among adults with normal BMI.
Associations extended across all eight outcomes, with the strongest findings for T2D.
The results support complementary assessment of body mass and central adiposity.
Normal BMI did not imply low adiposity-related risk (Sun et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Normal BMI did not imply low adiposity-related risk <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Sun et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Despite a modest BMI difference, the normal-BMI WHtR groups differed by 13.1 cm in waist circumference.
Elevated WHtR was associated with a 74% higher T2D hazard and approximately 50% higher MI and stroke hazards, accompanied by higher standardized event probabilities.
Previous studies demonstrated within-BMI heterogeneity using waist circumference or waist-to-hip ratio (Jayedi et al., 2022; Feng et al., 2024; Xue et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Previous studies demonstrated within-BMI heterogeneity using waist circumference or waist-to-hip ratio <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Jayedi et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Feng et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Xue et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Our contribution extends this evidence across prospective CKM outcomes, standardized event probabilities, and cross-validated discrimination.
BMI-category comparisons strengthen this interpretation.
Diabetes associations were stronger in normal BMI than obesity, although the comparison with overweight was inconclusive; hypertension associations were stronger than in both groups.
Findings persisted with flexible age adjustment and spline modeling (Supplemental Tables S3, S4, and S5).
text.formatted: Findings persisted with flexible age adjustment and spline modeling (Supplemental Tables <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">S3</ref>, <ref type="table">S4</ref>, and S5).

text.text: These relative associations do not establish greater absolute risk or intervention benefit in normal-BMI adults.
Normal BMI with elevated WHtR might reflect greater abdominal adiposity relative to peripheral lean tissue.
Lower muscle mass and insulin resistance could contribute to diabetes risk, but muscle mass, strength, insulin resistance, and diabetes mediation were not assessed.
These findings do not establish sarcopenia or a specific mechanism.
Flexible age adjustment was reassuring because elevated-WHtR normal-BMI adults were substantially older.
Associations also occurred in both sexes, with similar diabetes estimates despite a formal sex interaction and no sex interaction for the normal-BMI threshold contrast.

Exploratory racial differences could reflect body composition, social/environmental exposures, health care access, ascertainment, or residual confounding; they do not establish biological differences or justify race-specific WHtR thresholds.
Spline findings support treating WHtR as a continuum.
Risk did not change abruptly at 0.50, and HF and AF relationships were more curvilinear than those for T2D and hypertension.
Association does not establish prediction or clinical utility.
Cross-validated discrimination gains ranged from ΔC=0.0134 for T2D to 0.0009 for AF.
The smaller cardiovascular gains suggest limited additional rank-order discrimination beyond the included covariates (Wormser et al., 2011).
text.formatted: The smaller cardiovascular gains suggest limited additional rank-order discrimination beyond the included covariates <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Wormser et al., 2011</ref>).

text.text: WHtR appears useful as a complementary phenotype rather than a stand-alone risk model.
Several limitations apply.
The observational design precludes causal inference, and residual confounding by lifestyle, medications, family history, body composition, or health care utilization remains possible.
Blood pressure, glycemia, and lipids were omitted as potential mediators; their exclusion does not diminish their clinical predictive importance.
All of Us is a volunteer cohort, so the 31.3% prevalence is not a national estimate (AoURP Investigators, 2019).
Threshold transportability across populations remains uncertain because BMI-adiposity relationships vary (Deurenberg-Yap et al., 2000).
text.formatted: Threshold transportability across populations remains uncertain because BMI-adiposity relationships vary <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Deurenberg-Yap et al., 2000)</ref>.

text.text: Exploratory subgroup analyses involved multiple comparisons and cannot establish subgroup-specific thresholds.
Race and ethnicity are social classifications, and these analyses cannot separate contextual exposures from body composition or confounding.
EHR outcomes depend on coding, utilization, and observation continuity.

Pre-index observation and landmark restrictions reduce but do not eliminate unrecognized prevalent disease, near-term ascertainment, or prior disease-related changes in body composition (Supplemental Table S10).

Continuous WHtR associations with diabetes and hypertension were particularly pronounced among normal-BMI adults, although heterogeneity differed by outcome and model specification.
